Cross-lingual transfer analysis

Which language-level features govern how well mathematical reasoning transfers out of English? This implements the GLMM from analysis.md, from the raw instance table through to the fitted model, with inspection at each stage.

The document fits one model of final accuracy and one decomposition of where in a solution the transfer gap accrues. Everything else is an ablation against the first of those.

# The seven GLMM fits below take ~45 min in total, so the data-prep and fitting
# chunks are cached. Invalidation is explicit rather than trusted to knitr's
# code hashing:
#   - the prep chain carries cache.extra = md5 of the input files, so a
#     regenerated parquet forces a rebuild;
#   - the fit chunks carry cache.extra = RHS, the model formula string, so
#     editing the specification forces a refit even though the chunk code
#     itself is unchanged;
#   - dependson chains prep -> fits, so upstream changes propagate.
# cache.lazy = FALSE because the fitted merMod objects are large and lazy
# loading them is slower than reading them outright.
# Delete _cache/ to force a full rebuild.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  warning = FALSE, message = TRUE,
  cache.path = "_cache/transfer_analysis/",
  cache.lazy = FALSE
)

library(nanoparquet)
## Warning: package 'nanoparquet' was built under R version 4.5.2
library(dplyr)
## 
## Attaching package: 'dplyr'
## The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
## 
##     filter, lag
## The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
## 
##     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
library(stringr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

transfer_dir <- "../../artifacts/transfer_tables"
out_dir <- "../../artifacts/analysis"
dir.create(out_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

# Hashed into the prep chunks' cache keys.
input_fingerprint <- function() {
  tools::md5sum(c(file.path(transfer_dir, "analysis.parquet"), "recovered_fertility.csv"))
}

Configuration

SPLIT <- "synthetic" # "original" for the robustness check

# Excluded by base name (before the reasoning suffix), so each entry catches all
# of a model's reasoning variants.
#   gpt-5.4-nano - proprietary: no parameter count, closed tokenizer (so no
#                  fertility). Cannot enter a model with size or fertility terms.
EXCLUDED_MODELS <- c(
  "gpt-5.4-nano"
)

# eng_metric is English with metric units, not a language, and has no typological
# or resource features. uncorrected_isl is machine-translated Icelandic before
# human correction, kept in the dataset for the validation figure but not used in
# the analysis. English itself is kept -- it anchors the intercept at fertility 1,
# typological distance 0, maximum resource.
EXCLUDED_LANGUAGES <- c("eng_metric", "uncorrected_isl")

# Dataset revision. The parquet currently carries two:
#   refs/pr/16  - all 48 models x 16 languages, every cell n = 20. Complete and
#                 balanced.
#   d34a0ffc..  - a re-evaluation after the dan/deu/est/jpn template fixes, plus
#                 the new urd language. Partial: only 26 of 48 models for
#                 dan/deu/jpn and 17 for est.
# Pooling them would mix pre-fix and post-fix evaluations of the same templates
# (Qwen3-8B on deu scores .902 on pr16 and .920 on the pinned revision) and would
# triple-count some cells. We therefore pin to pr/16, which keeps the design
# balanced and isolates the one thing the refresh changed for us -- the number
# extraction fix, which was recomputed over every row regardless of revision.
#
# Consequences, to revisit once the re-evaluation is complete upstream:
#   - dan, deu, est and jpn use their pre-fix templates;
#   - urd is dropped (it exists only in the pinned revision, and has no
#     typological_distance or log10_common_crawl_pages in any case).
DATASET_REVISION <- "@refs/pr/16/"

Load the instance table

collect_transfer_tables.py writes one Parquet row per evaluated instance: correct as a logical, the reasoning mode in the model name, the number-parsing counts, and every feature we need – typological_distance, log10_common_crawl_pages, and the tokenizer fertilities. Normalised fertility is the model’s fertility relative to its own English fertility.

lhs_* and rhs_* are the equation-side counts: number_coverage_utils.py parses the gold solution’s <<lhs=rhs>> calculator annotations, so lhs_count is the operands a correct solution uses and rhs_count the intermediate results it produces; *_retrieved is how many of each appear in the model’s response. These drive the reasoning-ladder section.

STOPGAP: the current parquet has no tokenizer fertility at all – the column is NA for all 48 models, where the previous version had it for all but gemma-3 and EuroLLM-9B-Instruct. recovered_fertility.csv now carries the full 841 model-by-language table, lifted from the pre-refresh parquet (git 25f32c78^), and we coalesce it in.

This is exact rather than approximate: we pin to the refs/pr/16 revision below, and those rows are unchanged between the two parquet versions (identical row count and identical overall accuracy to six decimal places), so the tokenizer and the text a fertility is computed from are both identical. The join should be removed once the upstream fertility computation is restored.

recovered_fertility <- read.csv("recovered_fertility.csv")

observations <- read_parquet(file.path(transfer_dir, "analysis.parquet")) %>%
  select(
    source_id, language, correct, model, family, params_b, split, eval_id, task,
    typological_distance, log10_common_crawl_pages,
    tokenizer_fertility, english_fertility_tokens_per_character,
    all_prompt_numbers_present, prompt_number_count, retrieved_prompt_number_count,
    lhs_count, lhs_retrieved, rhs_count, rhs_retrieved
  ) %>%
  left_join(recovered_fertility, by = c("model", "language"), suffix = c("", "_rec")) %>%
  mutate(
    tokenizer_fertility = coalesce(tokenizer_fertility, tokenizer_fertility_rec),
    english_fertility_tokens_per_character =
      coalesce(english_fertility_tokens_per_character, english_fertility_tokens_per_character_rec),
    relative_fertility = tokenizer_fertility / english_fertility_tokens_per_character
  ) %>%
  select(-tokenizer_fertility_rec, -english_fertility_tokens_per_character_rec)

dim(observations)
## [1] 2086100      21

Reasoning mode

Reasoning mode is explicit in the model name. Qwen3 / Qwen3.5 label the reasoning-off runs, so the bare name is the reasoning-on run.

# Bases that appear with a "(reasoning off)" variant: their bare form is the
# reasoning-on run and should be labelled as such.
off_bases <- observations %>%
  filter(str_detect(model, "\\(reasoning off\\)$")) %>%
  mutate(base = str_remove(model, "\\s*\\(reasoning off\\)$")) %>%
  distinct(base) %>%
  pull(base)

observations <- observations %>%
  mutate(
    model = if_else(model %in% off_bases, paste0(model, " (reasoning on)"), model),
    base_model = str_remove(model, "\\s*\\(reasoning (on|off)\\)$")
  )

observations %>%
  filter(base_model %in% off_bases) %>%
  distinct(base_model, model) %>%
  arrange(base_model)

Filter to the analysis set

EXCLUDED_MODELS is matched on base_model, so it catches every reasoning variant of a listed model.

observations <- observations %>%
  filter(
    split == SPLIT,
    str_detect(task, fixed(DATASET_REVISION)),
    !language %in% EXCLUDED_LANGUAGES,
    !base_model %in% EXCLUDED_MODELS
  )

Feature coverage

observations %>%
  summarise(across(
    c(typological_distance, log10_common_crawl_pages, relative_fertility),
    ~ sum(is.na(.)), .names = "na_{.col}"
  ))
##   na_typological_distance na_log10_common_crawl_pages na_relative_fertility
## 1                       0                           0                     0

Aggregate to cells

One row per (model, language, template). Every predictor is constant within such a cell, so Binomial(n_total, pi) has the same likelihood as the individual Bernoulli draws at roughly 1/20th the rows – carried through with first().

cells <- observations %>%
  group_by(model, base_model, family, language, template = source_id) %>%
  summarise(
    n_correct = sum(correct),
    n_total = n(),
    params_b = first(params_b),
    typological_distance_from_english = first(typological_distance),
    log10_common_crawl_pages = first(log10_common_crawl_pages),
    relative_fertility = first(relative_fertility),
    # Equation-side counts for the reasoning ladder.
    n_lhs = sum(lhs_count),
    n_lhs_ret = sum(lhs_retrieved),
    n_rhs = sum(rhs_count),
    n_rhs_ret = sum(rhs_retrieved),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

dim(cells)
## [1] 76800    15
summary(cells$n_total)
##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
##      20      20      20      20      20      20

n_total is a uniform 20 per cell – the duplicate OLMo-2 evaluation runs that previously doubled three cells were removed upstream in collect_transfer_tables.py.

The design is balanced – every model seen in every language, 100 templates each:

Predictors

Standardise the continuous predictors so the interaction terms are interpretable at the mean and the weakly-informative priors are on a sensible scale.

Splitting relative fertility between and within language

Relative fertility – a model’s tokens-per-character on the target language divided by its own tokens-per-character on English – is the only language feature that is a property of the model rather than the language, and pooling those two roles is what made its coefficient uninterpretable in earlier versions of this analysis. We split it:

  • relative_fertility_between – the language’s mean relative fertility across models. A language-level quantity, and strongly collinear with typological distance (r ~ 0.8): languages that are structurally distant from English also tokenise badly in most models.
  • relative_fertility_within – a model’s deviation from that language mean. This is “this model tokenises this language worse than its peers do”, which is the quantity we actually have a mechanism for, and it is orthogonal by construction to every language-level predictor.

Only relative_fertility_within enters the model. The point of splitting was to get the collinearity out of the fertility estimate, and relative_fertility_between is the collinear part – entering it puts the problem straight back in. Two reasons it costs us nothing to drop:

  • relative_fertility_within is unaffected. The two arms are orthogonal by construction (r = 0.00), so removing one leaves the other’s estimate essentially unchanged.
  • Typological distance is improved. With relative_fertility_between in the model, the typological-distance coefficient is “the effect of structural distance holding between-language fertility constant” – a near-meaningless contrast when the two correlate at 0.8 over 16 languages, and one that inflates its standard error. Dropping it makes the coefficient the total language-level effect, which is both interpretable and better estimated.

The cost is that we can no longer claim to have tested a between-language fertility effect separately from typological distance. We could not have done so honestly anyway: at r = 0.8 on 16 points they are not separately identifiable, and the null we previously reported for relative_fertility_between was underdetermination rather than evidence of no effect. Typological distance should now be read as the language-level axis those two features jointly describe – structural distance from English, which travels with tokenising badly.

Note this is not a return to a single pooled fertility term. The split is still computed; we simply enter one arm of it. Pooling is what produced the wrong sign in earlier versions.

standardise <- function(x) as.numeric((x - mean(x)) / sd(x))

cells <- cells %>%
  group_by(language) %>%
  mutate(relative_fertility_between = mean(relative_fertility)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    relative_fertility_within = relative_fertility - relative_fertility_between,
    log2_params = log2(params_b),
    relative_fertility_between_z = standardise(relative_fertility_between),
    relative_fertility_within_z = standardise(relative_fertility_within),
    typological_distance_z = standardise(typological_distance_from_english),
    log_resource_z = standardise(log10_common_crawl_pages),
    log_params_z = standardise(log2_params),
    # base_model is the tokenizer/weights identity shared across reasoning modes;
    # reasoning is the on/off knob (non-reasoning models are "off").
    reasoning = factor(if_else(str_detect(model, "\\(reasoning on\\)$"), "on", "off"),
                       levels = c("off", "on"))
  ) %>%
  arrange(family, model, language, template)

cells %>%
  select(relative_fertility_within_z, relative_fertility_between_z, typological_distance_z,
         log_resource_z, log_params_z) %>%
  summary()

Two predictors are language-level, so their main effects rest on 16 points regardless of the 1.5M instances behind them. Worth seeing the collinearity before reading any coefficient:

cells %>%
  select(relative_fertility_within_z, relative_fertility_between_z, typological_distance_z,
         log_resource_z, log_params_z) %>%
  cor() %>%
  round(2)
##                              relative_fertility_within_z
## relative_fertility_within_z                         1.00
## relative_fertility_between_z                        0.00
## typological_distance_z                              0.00
## log_resource_z                                      0.00
## log_params_z                                        0.03
##                              relative_fertility_between_z
## relative_fertility_within_z                          0.00
## relative_fertility_between_z                         1.00
## typological_distance_z                               0.80
## log_resource_z                                      -0.35
## log_params_z                                         0.00
##                              typological_distance_z log_resource_z log_params_z
## relative_fertility_within_z                     0.0           0.00         0.03
## relative_fertility_between_z                    0.8          -0.35         0.00
## typological_distance_z                          1.0          -0.30         0.00
## log_resource_z                                 -0.3           1.00         0.00
## log_params_z                                    0.0           0.00         1.00
# and at the level the language predictors actually vary
cells %>%
  distinct(language, relative_fertility_between_z, typological_distance_z, log_resource_z) %>%
  select(-language) %>%
  cor() %>%
  round(2)
##                              relative_fertility_between_z
## relative_fertility_between_z                         1.00
## typological_distance_z                               0.80
## log_resource_z                                      -0.35
##                              typological_distance_z log_resource_z
## relative_fertility_between_z                    0.8          -0.35
## typological_distance_z                          1.0          -0.30
## log_resource_z                                 -0.3           1.00

The split does what it is meant to: relative_fertility_within is orthogonal (r = 0.00) to typological distance, resource and relative_fertility_between, so its coefficient is free of the collinearity problem. The r ~ 0.8 between relative_fertility_between and typological distance is the reason the between arm stays out of the model – it is displayed here so the reader can see what is being excluded and why, not because it is a candidate predictor.

cells %>%
  distinct(model, language, relative_fertility, typological_distance_from_english, log10_common_crawl_pages) %>%
  pivot_longer(c(relative_fertility, typological_distance_from_english, log10_common_crawl_pages)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(value, language)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~name, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "Feature spread across languages") +
  theme_minimal()

Raw accuracy by language and size, as a sanity check on what the model should recover.

Languages are ordered by resource level and coloured on a sequential ramp rather than with categorical hues: resource is a magnitude, so the colour should carry the ordering. The legend states each language’s absolute Common Crawl page count; the spread is large, from ~0.6M pages for Marathi to ~880M for English. mako runs dark to light through a single blue-green hue, is monotonic in lightness (so the order survives greyscale and colour-vision deficiency), and avoids the pale yellow end of viridis that disappears against a white panel. Highest-resource language is darkest.

language_levels <- cells %>%
  distinct(language, log10_common_crawl_pages) %>%
  arrange(desc(log10_common_crawl_pages))

# Label with the resource value so the legend states the ordering explicitly.
# Label with the absolute Common Crawl page count, so the legend states the
# ordering in a concrete unit rather than a log value or a ratio to English.
pages_lab <- function(l) {
  v <- 10^l
  ifelse(v >= 1e9, paste0(round(v/1e9, 1), "B"), paste0(round(v/1e6), "M"))
}
language_labels <- sprintf("%s (%s)", language_levels$language,
                           pages_lab(language_levels$log10_common_crawl_pages))
names(language_labels) <- language_levels$language

language_levels
## # A tibble: 16 × 2
##    language log10_common_crawl_pages
##    <chr>                       <dbl>
##  1 eng                          8.95
##  2 rus                          8.14
##  3 deu                          8.11
##  4 jpn                          8.07
##  5 fra                          8.01
##  6 zho                          8.01
##  7 ita                          7.73
##  8 nld                          7.60
##  9 ukr                          7.24
## 10 ara                          7.15
## 11 dan                          7.06
## 12 nob                          6.85
## 13 hin                          6.68
## 14 est                          6.49
## 15 isl                          5.89
## 16 mar                          5.81
cells %>%
  group_by(model, language, log2_params) %>%
  summarise(accuracy = sum(n_correct) / sum(n_total), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(language = factor(language, levels = language_levels$language)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(log2_params, accuracy, colour = language)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.85, size = 1.8) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(
    option = "mako", begin = 0.08, end = 0.82, direction = 1,
    labels = language_labels
  ) +
  # loess is unconstrained and overshoots 1.0 at the top end; clip the view
  # rather than the data so the smoother still sees every point.
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    x = "log2 parameters (B)", y = "accuracy",
    colour = "Language\n(Common Crawl pages)",
    title = "Transfer gap narrows with scale",
    subtitle = "Languages ordered by resource level, darkest = highest resource"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

The model

cells <- cells %>% mutate(across(c(model, base_model, family, language, template), as.factor))
saveRDS(cells, file.path(out_dir, "model_cells.rds"))

Random-effects structure

Four grouping factors, each of which corresponds to a level at which one of our predictors varies:

  • (1 | family/base_model) – model skill. base_model is the weights identity shared across reasoning modes.
  • (1 | model) – nested inside base_model, this is the reasoning variant. It matters because reasoning is a fixed effect that varies at exactly this level: without it, the reasoning main effect would be tested against cell noise rather than against how much reasoning helps across base models.
  • (1 | template) – item difficulty, the largest single component.
  • (1 | language) – the per-language residual, discussed below.
  • (1 | model:language) – model-specific transfer idiosyncrasy.

The (1 | language) term is the one worth justifying, because it is what makes the language-level coefficients honest rather than merely large. log_resource_z and typological_distance_z vary only across the 16 languages, but without a language intercept their standard errors are computed from the model:language stratum – roughly (models x languages) cells treated as independent evidence about a predictor with 16 actual points. That is pseudo-replication, and it does not wash out with more data at the instance or model level. The nolang comparison below quantifies what it costs.

The fixed-effect structure interacts the language features with size and with reasoning, because the question is not only whether each feature hurts but whether either of the two levers we can actually pull – scale, reasoning – narrows the gap it opens.

The specification lives in its own uncached chunk so that the formula strings are always in scope, and so that the fit chunks can key their cache on RHS: edit the model and every fit below rebuilds, leave it alone and none of them do.

library(lme4)
## Loading required package: Matrix
## 
## Attaching package: 'Matrix'
## The following objects are masked from 'package:tidyr':
## 
##     expand, pack, unpack
ctrl <- glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa", optCtrl = list(maxfun = 3e5))

RE <- "(1 | family/base_model) + (1 | model) + (1 | template) + (1 | language) + (1 | model:language)"
FEAT <- "(relative_fertility_within_z + typological_distance_z + log_resource_z)"
RHS <- paste(
  FEAT, "* log_params_z +",
  "reasoning * (relative_fertility_within_z +",
  "typological_distance_z + log_resource_z + log_params_z) +", RE
)

cat(RHS)
## (relative_fertility_within_z + typological_distance_z + log_resource_z) * log_params_z + reasoning * (relative_fertility_within_z + typological_distance_z + log_resource_z + log_params_z) + (1 | family/base_model) + (1 | model) + (1 | template) + (1 | language) + (1 | model:language)
fit_main <- glmer(
  as.formula(paste("cbind(n_correct, n_total - n_correct) ~", RHS)),
  data = cells, family = binomial(), control = ctrl
)
summary(fit_main)

Results

Size is the largest single effect (log_params_z ~ 1.88, p < 1e-16). Among the language features, resource level dominates (log_resource_z ~ 0.71, p < 1e-16): higher-resource languages are substantially easier. Typological distance hurts (~ -0.29, p = 1.5e-4), and within-language relative fertility hurts in the theoretically expected direction (~ -0.07, p = .019) – a model that tokenises a language worse than its peers do performs worse on it.

Read the typological-distance coefficient as the whole language-level axis of structural distance from English, which travels with tokenising that language badly (r ~ 0.8 between the two over our 16 languages). It is not a distance effect net of tokenisation; the design cannot separate those.

That sign on fertility is worth flagging: pooled fertility carried a positive coefficient in earlier versions of this analysis, which never made sense. It was an artifact of the between-language collinearity, and splitting the term both fixes the sign and explains the old result.

The interactions are where the actionable content sits, and the two levers behave differently:

  • Scale buffers resource. log_resource_z:log_params_z ~ -0.25, p < 1e-16. Larger models suffer less from a language being low-resource.
  • Scale does not buffer typological distance. ~ 0.02, p = .45. Nor fertility (p = .42).
  • Reasoning buffers resource. log_resource_z:reasoningon ~ -0.15, p = .004.
  • Reasoning also buffers typological distance. ~ +0.12, p = .013. The main effect is negative, so a positive interaction means the distance penalty shrinks when reasoning is on.

So scale helps only against data scarcity, while reasoning helps against both. Reasoning is the only lever here that does anything about structural distance – which is the more useful finding of the two, because distance is the feature you cannot change about a language.

A caveat on that last bullet, because it is new. In an earlier specification that also carried a between-language fertility term, this interaction was ~0.03 with p = .67, and the document concluded that neither lever touched structural distance. The two terms are collinear at r ~ 0.8 and were splitting one effect between them (relative_fertility_between:reasoning took ~0.12, p = .13). Dropping the between arm assigns it to typological distance, which is the interpretation the design supports – but it means the effect is identified off a language-level axis that confounds structural distance with tokenisation quality, and should be described that way rather than as “reasoning helps with grammar”.

Effect sizes in interpretable units

Coefficients are per standard deviation of a standardised predictor, which is convenient for fitting and useless for intuition. Both size and resource are log-transformed, so dividing by the SD puts them in doublings, and the two can then be quoted against each other.

Note that standardising makes the choice of log base irrelevant to the fit – z(log10 x) and z(log2 x) are the same vector to numerical precision – so this is purely a reporting transformation and changes nothing estimated above.

sd_p <- sd(cells$log2_params)
sd_r <- sd(cells$log10_common_crawl_pages)
b <- fixef(fit_main)

per_doubling_params <- b[["log_params_z"]] / sd_p
per_doubling_pages  <- b[["log_resource_z"]] / sd_r * log10(2)

tibble::tibble(
  quantity = c("per doubling of parameters", "per doubling of Common Crawl pages",
               "doublings of data equal to one doubling of parameters"),
  value = c(per_doubling_params, per_doubling_pages,
            per_doubling_params / per_doubling_pages)
)
## # A tibble: 3 × 2
##   quantity                                              value
##   <chr>                                                 <dbl>
## 1 per doubling of parameters                            0.990
## 2 per doubling of Common Crawl pages                    0.254
## 3 doublings of data equal to one doubling of parameters 3.90

Model size buys about 1.0 log-odds per doubling of parameters, and language resource about 0.25 log-odds per doubling of Common Crawl pages. So one doubling of model size is worth roughly four doublings of language data, i.e. about 15x the data – a convenient way to state the trade-off, and directly comparable to how scaling laws are usually reported.

The same exchange rate prices the language gaps themselves: the observed range of resource levels, English down to Marathi, costs about 2.7 doublings of model size (~6x the parameters), and the range of typological distance about 1.1 doublings (~2x).

Two caveats on these numbers. They use main effects at the sample means and therefore ignore the resource x size interaction, which makes the true exchange rate depend on model size; and Common Crawl pages is a proxy for a language’s share of the training mixture, not a measurement of it.

The reasoning main effect is not significant (~ 0.49, p = .12). This is a consequence of the (1 | model) term putting it on the correct stratum: it is tested against the 12 base models run both ways, which is genuinely thin evidence for an average lift. The claim this model supports is the interaction – reasoning differentially helps languages that are far from English on both axes – not “reasoning raises accuracy”. For the latter, the paired comparison further down is better evidence and does not depend on this specification at all.

How much transfer variation do the features explain?

With a language intercept present, the question splits into two, and they have very different answers.

vc <- function(f, g) attr(VarCorr(f)[[g]], "stddev")[[1]]

tibble(
  component = c("language", "model:language"),
  sd_baseline = c(vc(fit_baseline, "language"), vc(fit_baseline, "model:language")),
  sd_full = c(vc(fit_main, "language"), vc(fit_main, "model:language"))
) %>%
  mutate(variance_explained = 1 - sd_full^2 / sd_baseline^2)
## # A tibble: 2 × 4
##   component      sd_baseline sd_full variance_explained
##   <chr>                <dbl>   <dbl>              <dbl>
## 1 language             0.831   0.272              0.893
## 2 model:language       0.649   0.580              0.199
  • Between-language variance: ~89% explained (SD 0.83 -> 0.27). Almost all of why some languages are harder than others is captured by resource level, typological distance and fertility.
  • Model-by-language variance: ~20% explained (SD 0.65 -> 0.58). Which model struggles with which language, beyond that language’s general difficulty, is largely unexplained. relative_fertility_within is the only predictor operating at this level and its effect is small.

The second number is a real negative result and belongs in the write-up: language features are close to sufficient for language difficulty, and close to useless for model-specific transfer failure.

Note that earlier versions of this analysis reported a single pooled figure (~64% of sd(model:language)) because there was no language intercept to separate the two components; that number is not comparable to either of these.

Which languages do we predict poorly?

ranef(fit_main)$language %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("language") %>%
  arrange(`(Intercept)`)
##    language (Intercept)
## 1       rus -0.44707052
## 2       deu -0.33854145
## 3       isl -0.28243253
## 4       est -0.24248930
## 5       mar -0.12567833
## 6       jpn -0.10013604
## 7       nld -0.05806610
## 8       eng -0.01665381
## 9       hin  0.01380465
## 10      fra  0.01549329
## 11      ukr  0.03346699
## 12      zho  0.20186606
## 13      dan  0.22052842
## 14      ita  0.29937366
## 15      ara  0.38896424
## 16      nob  0.43836131

The features over-predict rus, deu, isl and est, and under-predict nob, ara, ita and dan. Russian is the striking case: second-highest resource and low typological distance, so the model expects a great deal and does not get it.

There is a candidate explanation worth one follow-up. The languages that over-perform their predictions – Norwegian, Danish, Italian – all have close, high-resource relatives (Swedish/German/English; French/Spanish), while our features only measure distance to English. A resource-weighted typological proximity to the whole training mix, rather than to English alone, would test that. Treat it as a hypothesis: 16 shrunken residuals will support many stories.

zho at +0.14 is consistent with Common Crawl page counts underestimating Chinese resource, which is a known weakness of the proxy.

What the language intercept costs

Refitting the identical model without (1 | language) isolates the effect of using the wrong error stratum.

)

## log_params_z:reasoningon                  0.3093 0.2987   0.9918

The result is about as clean as this kind of check gets: standard errors inflate by ~2.6x on exactly the two language-level predictors and are unchanged (0.90-1.00x) on every other term. Point estimates barely move (log_resource_z 0.7092 -> 0.7119, typological_distance_z -0.2882 -> -0.2876), so this is purely an inference correction, not a different answer.

The consequential case is typological distance: z = -9.8 without the intercept, -3.8 with it. Both are significant, but the first overstates the evidence by a factor the design does not support. Resource behaves the same way (z = 24.1 to 9.4) and survives comfortably either way.

Ablations

Two additions the earlier analysis flagged as promising. Both are null once tested on the correct stratum with 16 languages.

Resource x typological distance

Does a high resource level buffer the typological-distance penalty?

fit_rxt <- update(fit_main, . ~ . + typological_distance_z:log_resource_z)

Script

script was previously dropped as unidentifiable. With 7 non-Latin languages out of 16 it now is identifiable, though the leverage is thin: it comes almost entirely from Cyrillic rus/ukr (non-Latin but typologically close to English) against Latin-script est (typologically distant).

non_latin <- c("ara", "hin", "jpn", "mar", "rus", "ukr", "urd", "zho")
cells_script <- cells %>%
  mutate(non_latin = factor(if_else(language %in% non_latin, "yes", "no"), levels = c("no", "yes")))

fit_script <- glmer(as.formula(paste("cbind(n_correct, n_total - n_correct) ~ non_latin +", RHS)),
                    data = cells_script, family = binomial(), control = ctrl)
round(summary(fit_script)$coefficients[c("non_latinyes", "typological_distance_z"), , drop = FALSE], 4)

Also null (~ -0.03, p = .90). Note the converse is informative too: typological distance barely moves when script is added (-0.29 -> -0.28, still p < .05), so the typological-distance effect is not a writing-system effect in disguise. The URIEL distance we use is cosine distance from English over the 103-feature syntax_knn vector – purely morphosyntactic (word order, adposition and adjective order, case marking), a property of the spoken language – so it carries no orthographic information to begin with.

Note that transferfeatures.py describes this feature in its module docstring and in the exported feature_sources.json as concatenating syntax_knn and inventory_knn. The code does not: collect_language_features() requests syntax_knn alone, and records the accurate label in typological_feature_set. The prose provenance is stale and should be corrected upstream.

Reasoning and the transfer gap

Because reasoning is a knob rather than a property of a language, its average effect is clearest from the paired models directly – reasoning on versus off, across the base models run both ways.

paired_bases <- cells %>%
  distinct(base_model, reasoning) %>%
  count(base_model) %>%
  filter(n == 2) %>%
  pull(base_model)

by_lang <- cells %>%
  filter(base_model %in% paired_bases) %>%
  group_by(reasoning, language) %>%
  summarise(acc = sum(n_correct) / sum(n_total), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(logit = qlogis(acc))

english <- by_lang %>% filter(language == "eng") %>% select(reasoning, eng_acc = acc, eng_logit = logit)

by_lang %>%
  filter(language != "eng") %>%
  left_join(english, by = "reasoning") %>%
  group_by(reasoning) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_accuracy       = mean(acc),
    gap_accuracy_points = mean(eng_acc - acc),      # absolute: English minus target
    # Two relative measures, because they are NOT the same and the difference
    # is large at our accuracy levels. The odds ratio is what the GLMM is linear
    # in; the risk ratio is what the phrase "times more likely to be wrong"
    # actually means. Reporting the former with the latter's wording overstates
    # the gap by 40-85% here.
    odds_ratio          = mean(exp(eng_logit - logit)),
    risk_ratio          = mean((1 - acc) / (1 - eng_acc))
  )
## # A tibble: 2 × 5
##   reasoning mean_accuracy gap_accuracy_points odds_ratio risk_ratio
##   <fct>             <dbl>               <dbl>      <dbl>      <dbl>
## 1 off               0.624               0.206       3.11       2.21
## 2 on                0.694               0.129       2.12       1.74

Turning reasoning on raises accuracy across the board (0.62 to 0.69, ~+7 points) and shrinks the English-to-target gap from 20.6 to 12.9 accuracy points. It also shrinks on the relative scale, on both of the measures below: with reasoning off a model is on average 2.2x more likely to answer incorrectly in a non-English language than in English, falling to 1.7x with reasoning on; on the odds scale the same comparison is 3.1x falling to 2.1x.

Keep those two apart. “Times more likely to be wrong” is a risk ratio; the GLMM is linear in the odds ratio, and at our accuracy levels they diverge badly – 3.1 versus 2.2 on average, and 6.0 versus 3.2 for Marathi. Quoting an odds ratio with risk-ratio wording is the standard misreading and inflates the claim substantially, so state which one is meant. We report the risk ratio, as the quantity the plain-language phrasing actually names.

One consequence to keep in view when reading the figures against the coefficient table. A risk ratio depends on the base rate it is measured against: at 32B the English error rate is ~7%, so a given absolute drop in accuracy produces a larger ratio than the same drop at 4B, where the English error rate is far higher. On the risk-ratio scale the large model therefore shows the steeper resource slope, while the fitted interaction – estimated on the odds scale – is log_resource_z:log_params_z = -0.25, meaning scale reduces the resource penalty. Both are correct statements about different quantities. The inferential claim is the coefficient; the risk-ratio figure is the descriptive one.

The distinction between the two gap measures matters. A uniform lift narrows the absolute gap on its own, because the accuracy scale compresses near the ceiling, while leaving the error-odds ratio unchanged. The ratio falling from 3.1 to 2.1 means reasoning does more than raise all boats – and the fitted term behind that is the reasoning x resource interaction in the main model (~ -0.13, p = .009).

This paired comparison, not the model’s reasoning main effect, is the right evidence for “reasoning helps”. The two answer different questions and both belong in the paper.

Where in the solution does the gap accrue?

The earlier version of this section asked a binary question – is the gap about parsing the problem or doing the maths? – using whether the response reproduced the prompt’s numbers. The equation-side counts let us ask a graded version instead, which is both sharper and avoids a serious measurement problem with the prompt-number metric (see the caveat at the end of this section).

Three rungs, increasing in depth through the solution:

  1. LHS – the operands a correct solution uses. Roughly “did the model take in the right inputs?”
  2. RHS – the intermediate results a correct solution produces. “Did the model actually compute the intervening steps?”
  3. Final answer – correct, i.e. the main model above.

All three are marginal, not conditional: rung 2 does not condition on having passed rung 1. So the ladder measures total accumulated degradation at increasing depth, which is what we want for a claim about compounding, and it avoids conditioning on a post-treatment variable.

cells %>%
  group_by(language) %>%
  summarise(
    lhs_rate = sum(n_lhs_ret) / sum(n_lhs),
    rhs_rate = sum(n_rhs_ret) / sum(n_rhs),
    accuracy = sum(n_correct) / sum(n_total),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(accuracy))

lhs_count and rhs_count are near-identical across all 16 languages and only ~2% of cells have no chevrons, uniformly distributed, so the denominators are comparable and the rungs measure what we intend.

fit_lhs <- glmer(as.formula(paste("cbind(n_lhs_ret, n_lhs - n_lhs_ret) ~", RHS)),
                 data = filter(cells, n_lhs > 0), family = binomial(), control = ctrl)

fit_rhs <- glmer(as.formula(paste("cbind(n_rhs_ret, n_rhs - n_rhs_ret) ~", RHS)),
                 data = filter(cells, n_rhs > 0), family = binomial(), control = ctrl)

The comparison that matters is across rungs, so the side-by-side comes first; the two fits in full follow.

                  "log_resource_z", "log_params_z", "log_resource_z:log_params_z")

Reading the ladder

Every coefficient grows along the chain: typological distance -0.09 -> -0.17 -> -0.29 (3.2x end to end), resource 0.30 -> 0.42 -> 0.71 (2.4x), within-language relative fertility -0.03 -> -0.07 -> -0.07 (2.0x). Size grows fastest (0.49 -> 0.93 -> 1.88, 3.8x), as does the size-buffers-resource interaction (-0.07 -> -0.12 -> -0.25).

The marginal ladder cannot, on its own, establish that this is compounding. The three outcomes have different base rates and different residual dispersion, so logit coefficients are not directly comparable in magnitude across them. A pure scale difference between the outcomes would inflate every coefficient by roughly a common factor – which is very close to what we observe. There is no feature here that stays flat and could serve as an internal control.

An earlier version of this analysis did report such a control: typological distance appeared flat across the rungs (-0.28, -0.27, -0.29) while resource tripled, and the contrast was read as evidence that structural distance is a cost paid once at input while data scarcity accumulates. That pattern was an artifact of a number-extraction bug. Japanese is the most typologically distant language in the set, and unmatched kanji numerals artificially depressed its LHS and RHS rates – the two rungs that depend on extracting numbers from responses – which inflated the typological-distance coefficient at exactly those rungs. With the extraction fixed, Japanese moves from 0.68/0.59 to 0.78/0.64 and the coefficient at the LHS rung drops by two thirds. The conclusion did not survive the fix, and the “fixed tax versus accumulating penalty” reading should not be quoted from earlier drafts – typological distance is now the fastest-growing of the three, the opposite of what that reading claimed.

So read the ladder as descriptive: the gap widens with depth on the raw rates (English to Marathi runs 0.19 at LHS, 0.30 at RHS, 0.36 at the final answer), and leave the question of why to the adjusted analysis below, which compares coefficients within a single outcome and is not exposed to the scale objection.

sd(language) also grows along the ladder (0.14 -> 0.16 -> 0.27), and the family variance collapses to the boundary at the LHS rung – model family is irrelevant to retrieving numbers and dominant for arithmetic. That last contrast is on the same scale caveat, but a variance component going to zero is not a matter of degree.

sdl <- function(f, g) attr(VarCorr(f)[[g]], "stddev")[[1]]
tibble(
  rung = c("lhs", "rhs", "final"),
  language = c(sdl(fit_lhs, "language"), sdl(fit_rhs, "language"), sdl(fit_main, "language")),
  model_language = c(sdl(fit_lhs, "model:language"), sdl(fit_rhs, "model:language"), sdl(fit_main, "model:language")),
  family = c(sdl(fit_lhs, "family"), sdl(fit_rhs, "family"), sdl(fit_main, "family"))
)

## 2 rhs      0.163          0.390 0.541   
## 3 final    0.272          0.580 1.33

Per-step versus accumulated

The marginal ladder cannot separate two mechanisms: each reasoning step being individually harder in low-resource languages, versus each step being equally hard with the deficit simply accumulating over more steps.

Conditioning hard on a full operand parse does not work as a test. Among instances where every operand was retrieved, the RHS rate is ~97% – at ceiling, with nothing left to explain – and the conditioning is severely differential across languages (full-LHS rates run from ~0.34 for mar to ~0.61 for eng), so it would compare the top third of one language against the top two thirds of another. That is selection on a collider, and it would produce a table that looks meaningful and is not.

Adjusting for operand retrieval instead of conditioning on it keeps the full sample and avoids the ceiling. It is still mediator adjustment, so the coefficient is not a clean causal effect, but it is statistically well behaved.

cells_adj <- cells %>%
  filter(n_lhs > 0, n_rhs > 0) %>%
  mutate(lhs_rate_z = as.numeric(scale(n_lhs_ret / n_lhs)))

fit_rhs_adj <- glmer(
  as.formula(paste("cbind(n_rhs_ret, n_rhs - n_rhs_ret) ~ lhs_rate_z +", RHS)),
  data = cells_adj, family = binomial(), control = ctrl
)
tt <- c("log_resource_z", "typological_distance_z", "relative_fertility_within_z")
round(data.frame(
  unadjusted = summary(fit_rhs)$coefficients[tt, 1],
  adjusted = summary(fit_rhs_adj)$coefficients[tt, 1],
  adj_se = summary(fit_rhs_adj)$coefficients[tt, 2],
  adj_p = summary(fit_rhs_adj)$coefficients[tt, 4]
), 4)

All three language features behave the same way: most of their effect on producing intermediate results is inherited from how well the operands were read, and a small but statistically clear residual survives.

feature unadjusted adjusted share propagated adjusted p
log_resource_z 0.420 0.099 76% < 1e-4
typological_distance_z -0.172 -0.075 56% < 1e-4
relative_fertility_within_z -0.067 -0.033 50% .005

Because this comparison is made within a single outcome, it is not exposed to the cross-outcome scale objection that limits the marginal ladder, which is why it carries the interpretation:

The transfer gap is predominantly a failure to take in the problem correctly. Once a model has read the operands, its remaining per-step disadvantage is real but small – roughly a quarter to a half of the raw effect.

This is consistent with the conditional descriptive above: among instances where every operand was retrieved, intermediate results follow ~97% of the time regardless of language. The arithmetic itself is close to language-invariant; what differs is getting the right numbers into it.

The three features differ in degree rather than kind, and the ordering is interpretable: resource is the most propagated (76%), typological distance less so (56%), fertility least (50%). Data scarcity does most of its damage by the model failing to take the problem in; structural distance and bad tokenisation keep more of a per-step penalty. The gap between 56% and 50% rests on the two smallest coefficients in the model, so treat that end of the ordering as suggestive.

Two caveats, and the second cuts against the residuals:

  1. This is mediator adjustment, not identified mediation. Anything affecting both operand retrieval and intermediate production without being in the model – item-specific model competence, say – can bias the adjusted coefficients. The random effects absorb some of this but not all.
  2. lhs_rate_z measures operand retrieval imperfectly, and adjusting for a noisily measured mediator under-adjusts. The residual direct effects are therefore biased away from zero, so the adjusted column is best read as an upper bound on the true per-step penalties. The propagated shares are correspondingly lower bounds – the reading-stage story is if anything stronger than the table shows.

Caveat: the prompt-number metric is not usable

The previous version of this section used all_prompt_numbers_present. It is still not usable for Japanese, though the failure mode has changed.

The prompt numbers are recovered by extracting from the prompt text, so the metric is only comparable across languages if extraction is equally reliable in each. It was not. In the earlier parquet, Japanese kanji numerals went unmatched and ~93% of Japanese prompts yielded zero extractable numbers (mean 0.08 against 3.24 for English); because an empty set evaluated vacuously true, Japanese was recorded as the best-parsing language in the study, above English.

The upstream refresh fixed the under-extraction, and fixed it broadly: ara (2.74 -> 3.22), nld (3.08 -> 3.23), ita (3.07 -> 3.22) and zho (3.13 -> 3.26) all moved into line, and fifteen of sixteen languages now sit within 0.13 numbers per template of English.

Japanese overshot. It now extracts 4.37 numbers per prompt against English’s 3.24 – an excess of 1.13 per template, on 82 of 100 templates – with retrieved_prompt_number_count inflated to match (3.91 against 3.10). The templates are identical across languages, so this is spurious matching, and kanji numerals inside ordinary words are the obvious candidate: 一緒, 一番, 十分 and 二人 all contain characters that are numerals standing alone. The bias has flipped sign rather than disappeared – more spurious prompt numbers makes “all present” harder to satisfy, so Japanese should now look artificially bad where it previously looked artificially good.

# The templates are shared, so prompt_number_count should be language-invariant.
# Any language far from the others is an extraction artifact, not a finding.
cells_pn <- observations %>%
  group_by(language) %>%
  summarise(mean_prompt_numbers = mean(prompt_number_count),
            mean_retrieved = mean(retrieved_prompt_number_count),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(mean_prompt_numbers))
cells_pn

The ladder is unaffected by any of this, which is why it is the instrument this document uses. Its denominators come from the gold solution’s <<lhs=rhs>> chevrons, which are written in ASCII digits in every language – verified language-invariant in the validation chunk above – and its numerators from model responses, which use ASCII digits too. Japanese sits mid-table on both rungs, in line with its accuracy.

Notes and limitations

Our resource proxy is Common Crawl page count. While probably close to real-world distributions, it likely has systematic bias (Chinese looks underestimated, and its positive language residual is consistent with that) and does not vary across model. Ideally this analysis would use models whose training distribution is known.

The reasoning main effect is identified from the 12 base models run both ways; Olmo-3-7B-Think is reasoning-on only and contributes only between-base information. Worth confirming the coefficient is stable on paired bases alone.
